doc.title: Clay Jenkins interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, March 18, 2016

title: The Delta blues as the root of American music
summary: He talks about the heartfelt nuance of the Delta players, introducing students to them, and the blues as the common denominator of American music.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: What the blues is, and why every jazz player needs it

blocks.x: And there’s only three beats in that bar.
Yeah. Like you have to get over that.

Exactly. But it’s just so heartfelt and the nuance was so amazing. And they were living that and — I introduced some of my young trumpet players at Eastman to some of this stuff and I had this kid come up to me and he said, “I don’t like this stuff but I sure am glad you’re playing it for me.” And I thought man, I was the same way. But I mean it’s not the beginning of the blues certainly. Because that was in the 30s when those guys were — you know. And then Muddy Waters kind of took that to Chicago and then that was another thing with electric guitars and everything. But that Delta thing just really hit home with me, and I feel like it made me a little bit more — it had more validity as a player. I’m very interested in African-American culture anyway. I always have been. And that was sort of the heart of the south in a really rough time. And so much of our music, whether it be country-western or blues or jazz or pop or R&B, it’s all got that in it. So it’s such a common denominator in American music, the essence of the blues. It’s so important. We wouldn’t have music if it wasn’t for that.
I forget how many times I’ve read this quote that goes something like, “jazz is America’s only true art form.” And I always say, “what about the blues?”
Well it came from the blues. It came from the blues. Yeah.
